s09.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:10 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN TABLE — LUC
body: He can’t sleep. The phone has been in the front pocket of his jeans since Canal, and he can feel it against his hip through the sleeping bag, warm from him, a coal he hasn’t taken out.

He goes down the attic stairs in his socks, backward, the way they have to be gone down, a hand on each rail. At the foot of them Mémère is asleep on the daybed with her lamp off and her hands folded on her beads on top of the quilt, very small under it, her mouth a little open. He goes past her on the boards that don’t talk and down the hall of First Communions toward the one light left on in the house.

The kitchen light is on. Luc sits at the table in a white undershirt and the dark blue trousers of his uniform. His duty belt hangs off the back of the chair beside him with everything still on it, and his shirt hangs off the chair on the other side, the radio clipped to its shoulder and turned down to a murmur: a dispatcher a long way off, reading numbers to somebody else. In front of him is the plate his mother left in the oven under foil. The masking tape that said LUC on the Tupperware has gone across onto the foil, and the foil is folded back off red beans and rice, a piece of the pickled pork, the heel of the French bread. He eats fast and neat, the fork never resting. Aints III lies under his chair with his chin on Luc’s sock.
Luc looks up at him in the hall door, and at the gold still on his cheekbone.
“Sit.”

Jack sits. Luc reaches behind him without getting up and opens the refrigerator, and an Abita comes out of it and across the oilcloth, the cap knocked off against the table’s edge with the heel of his hand on the way. Jack takes it. He drinks a little and holds the rest.
“Sixteen hours,” Luc says. “Canal.”
“I saw you. You nodded.”

“I saw you.” Luc tears the bread. A piece of the pork goes down under the chair, and the dog takes it and puts his chin back on the sock. “We lost one tonight. Seventy-one years old. Went down when the trophy came by. His heart. On his feet, in his Saints jacket, with his daughter hanging on to his arm. Took EMS twenty minutes to get through to him. He was gone before they got there. Maybe before he got to the street.”
He eats.

“Natural causes,” Luc says. “That’s what it was. That’s all the report’s ever going to say, and it’s true. And his daughter’s going to tell it at Thanksgiving for forty years. *He died at the parade.*” He runs the bread round the rim of the plate. “That’s a good one. That’s one you don’t mind writing.”
The refrigerator hums. On the chair back, the dispatcher says a street name to nobody in particular and lets go of the key. Jack works his thumbnail under the corner of the Abita’s label.
“Y’all go back to California next week,” Luc says.
“After Ash Wednesday.”
“Okay.” Luc nods at the plate, and the fork stops for the first time since Jack came in.

“First year I was on,” he says. “Spring of ’06. Gentilly. A man came back from Houston to gut his house. Everybody was gutting. He took it down to the studs by himself: the drywall, the carpet, the cabinets, the bed. Put it all out on the curb in a pile higher than his truck, and his wife stayed with her sister in Houston till he had it done. Gas came back on that block in March.” A forkful. “One night in April he sat down in what was left of his kitchen, and he didn’t turn the stove off.”
The label comes away under Jack’s thumbnail in a strip, soft from the cold, and he keeps going.

“There was a paper on the table,” Luc says. “Could’ve been a note. Could’ve been a list for Home Depot. The house was still wet; the paper was wet. My sergeant read it. I read it. You couldn’t have told anybody what it said.” He turns the fork over in his fingers and puts it down. “He wrote it *accidental*. So the wife could have the funeral Mass at St. Raphael’s with nobody whispering in the back pews. And so the policy would pay.”
The refrigerator shudders and goes quiet, and the kitchen is louder without it.
“Nobody lied,” Luc says. “He just didn’t write down what nobody could prove.”
He picks the fork back up and finishes the rice. Out in the front room the daybed creaks under Mémère and settles. Jack has the label off now. It lies on the oilcloth beside the bottle in a wet curl.
“You write some of them,” Luc says, to the last of the beans, “the way the family can live with.”

He wipes the plate clean with the heel of the bread and eats that too. When he looks up again it’s with the other look, the one from the cruiser window on Esplanade, and it goes to Jack’s face and stays on the left side of it, on the eyebrow, where the white line cuts through it and the hair never came back.
“Where’d you get that?”

journal.title: Luc Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s oldest brother; NOPD. Worked a barricade on Canal for the parade and nodded at us once across the street. At one in the morning he ate his mother’s plate at the kitchen table and told me two stories. You write some of them the way the family can live with. He doesn’t do that off the clock.

choices.key: At one in the morning at the Broussards’ kitchen table, Luc asked about your eyebrow. A fight, you said. A long time ago. You didn’t win. Nobody does, he said.
response: “A fight,” Jack says. “A long time ago.”
“You win?”
“No.”
Luc keeps the look on him a while, the same one, up from under his own eyebrows. “Nobody does.” He pushes his chair back. “I don’t do that off the clock.”

He rinses the plate at the sink and stands it in the rack. He puts the belt on standing up, by the back door, and it goes round him with everything on it, the leather creaking, and his hands do the buckle without him; then the shirt over the undershirt, the radio back on his shoulder, still talking. He has his hand on the back door before he says it.
“She’ll be down in a minute. She don’t sleep after a parade.”
The yard takes him. Jack sits with two-thirds of an Abita and a curl of wet label, and the dog under the empty chair.

choices.key: At one in the morning at the Broussards’ kitchen table, Luc asked about your eyebrow. You told him a nun did it, in third grade, with a ruler. Uh huh, he said.
response: “A nun,” Jack says. “Third grade. A ruler.”
“Uh huh.” Luc picks his teeth with a fingernail and gives that the length of time it deserves. “I don’t do that off the clock.”

He takes the plate to the sink, runs the water on it, and stands it in the rack. He gets into the shirt and the belt by the back door, and then his keys come out of the trouser pocket, a ring of them as big as a janitor’s, and he goes round it with his thumb in the light from the window till he has the one he wants. He holds it up like a thing he means to show Jack, and doesn’t.
“She’ll be down in a minute. She don’t sleep after a parade.”
Out front a truck door goes, and then an engine, going away up Dupre. The dog comes out from under the empty chair and lies down under Jack’s.

choices.key: At one in the morning at the Broussards’ kitchen table, Luc asked about your eyebrow. A jealous husband, you said, in Erie. He’s heard better at Central Lockup.
response: “A jealous husband,” Jack says. “Erie, Pennsylvania.”
“Erie.”
“Pennsylvania.”
“I’ve heard better at Central Lockup.” Luc doesn’t smile. Something at the corner of his mouth thinks about it and decides against. “I don’t do that off the clock.”

He rinses the plate and stands it in the rack, and dresses for the street by the back door, the belt, the shirt, the radio back on his shoulder. At the door his hand goes to the light switch beside the frame and stops there, and comes away, and he leaves the kitchen lit.
“She’ll be down in a minute. She don’t sleep after a parade.”
The back steps take his weight one at a time, and the yard has him, and the light stays on over the oilcloth for whoever it was left on for.

body: She comes down the hall in Remy’s LSU sweatshirt and bare feet, and the linoleum must be cold, because she crosses it on the outside edges of them to the stove. Her hair is down and flattened on one side from the pillow. She doesn’t say anything to him. She takes the small pot off its nail, not the big one, and the milk out of the refrigerator, and warms it on the low blue ring, because that’s how Mémère does it, with a pinch of sugar from the bowl and her back to him, stirring with a teaspoon so it won’t catch.

body.text: The crawfish he painted on her cheekbone is half gone, scrubbed at and given up on; one curl of it is left, gold, by her ear. His own is still on him. He can feel it pull when he moves his face.
body.else: There’s gold in her hairline still, from the twins and the brush, a fleck at her temple she missed. His own fleur-de-lis is still on him. He can feel it pull when he moves his face.

body: She pours two cups. She puts one down in front of him on top of the wet curl of label without asking, and sits across the oilcloth with the other in both hands, and sets her LG down face-up by the sugar bowl. Laney’s gold strand is still doubled round her wrist from Canal, and it clicks against the cup. Her fingers go to her collarbone, to the place the medal lives, and find the neck of Remy’s sweatshirt, and come back to the cup.
“Was that Luc’s truck?”
“He ate.”

“He always eats.” She blows on the milk. “He texted Mama about the man at the trophy float. Mama texted me. On his feet, on Canal, with the trophy going by.” She crosses herself with the cup still in her hand, quickly, the way she does at a siren, and looks up at the ceiling. “Not a bad way to go, Lord, if You were asking. Which You weren’t.”
She drinks. He drinks. It’s too sweet and it’s exactly right.
“Wes looked thin,” she says.
“He came.”
Lena looks at him over the cup, and nods, slowly, like that was the right answer to something.

“And Remy,” she says, picking it up from wherever it was before she came downstairs, “swears that ladder on Canal is his by right because he carried it from the truck, when Daddy carried it from the truck, and Remy carried the *cooler*, the empty cooler, and then he stood on the top step for the length of the Brees float like it was him getting saluted —”
On the oilcloth by the sugar bowl the LG lights up. The little screen on its outside says JULIAN.
She looks at it. She puts two fingers on the back of the phone and turns it over, face-down, without opening it, and the light goes out under it against the oilcloth.
“— and if he tries it again I’m knocking him off it myself.”

She drinks her milk. A minute goes, and the phone buzzes once more, face-down, rattling against the oilcloth toward the sugar bowl, and her hand comes down flat on it and keeps it still against the table until it stops. She leaves the hand where it is after that, and finishes the milk with the other one.

response: “Goodnight, Lena.”
She looks at him across the table, with the cup at her mouth, for long enough that he thinks she isn’t going to answer. “Night, Jack,” she says.
She takes the phone with her. He looks at the pot on the back of the stove, where the last of the milk has gone to skin.
“Your milk’s going to skin.”
“Let it.”

She stands up and drinks it off standing, skin and all, and makes a face at him over the bottom of the cup. She rinses the cup and stands it upside down in the rack beside Luc’s plate, and takes her phone with her.
He gets up and takes the small pot off the stove, and runs the water into it, and works the skin off the bottom with his thumb.
She lets him. Behind him a chair scrapes. “Night, Youngstown.”
When he turns from the sink with the pot dripping in his hand, the sugar bowl is where the phone was.

s10.slug: WEDNESDAY · 2:05 AM · THE ATTIC — SOMETHING FROM VANCOUVER
body: Back past the daybed at the foot of the stairs, where Mémère sleeps with her beads, and up the stairs a rung at a time with his hands, and his head up through the hatch into the cold. The box fan is off. Tonight the cold has come in under the roof instead, and the points of the nails over his mattress have each got a bead of it.

Kevin is asleep by the hatch on his back, zipped to the chin, with the rosary shut in his fist on his chest. Theo lies on the middle mattress with his hands folded and his face to the rafters, very still. Asleep, or doing a good impression of it; Jack can’t tell which, and doesn’t try.
He lies down under Remy’s Tiger and gets the RAZR out of his jeans at last, and opens it under the sleeping bag on its cracked hinge, and the screen lights his hands green.
*SKYE (MISFIT) · New Picture Msg · 6:55 PM.* The little envelope with the paperclip on it, unopened. Under it, the texts that came with it, the ones the phone could carry without asking him anything.

body.text: dont open this in front of anybody. i mean it this time
i was thinking about the darkroom. this is your fault
not for posting. not for anybody. yours

body: In the duffel by his head the swing print is still in Hale’s *Moviegoer*, face-down, NOT FOR POSTING across the back of it in her Sharpie.

*The darkroom.* The red bulb and the timer going, the prints of him drying on their line over the iron daybed, and *No.*, the first one she ever said to him and meant. He has carried that since Friday out of the house on Del Playa and down the length of Interstate 10 in a van with five other people in it, and up these stairs tonight, and it is still exactly as close as it was.

The streetlight comes in through the gable window past the dead fan and lies across the foot of his mattress. Kevin breathes, and turns over once in his sleeping bag with a sound like a grocery sack, and is still. The cold beads on the nails. He holds the phone under the sleeping bag with his thumb over the key.

choices.key: At two in the morning in the Broussards’ attic you opened what Skye sent from Vancouver. It was yours.
response: He opens it.

The RAZR goes to work on it, and it comes down the little screen from the top a band at a time, postage-stamp small, gray and then less gray, and he brings the phone out from under the sleeping bag and tilts it up to the streetlight until the grain settles. The first band is plaid. He knows it before anything else in it, the elbow worn thin: his shirt, which wardrobe must have given up for a night, spread out flat under her on a hotel bed, the collar turned up by her cheek. Then her face, upside down to him until he turns the phone, because she took it from above, blind, the 3GS held out over herself at the end of her arm, so the frame runs crooked down the length of the bed toward a gray window and her own forearm cuts across one corner of it, huge and out of focus. Her head is pushed back off the pillow. Her eyes are shut and her mouth is open. Every one she has ever sent him knew exactly where his eyes would be — dared them, asked them, laughed at them — and this one isn’t looking for anybody at all. Down the length of her, past her breasts and the long bare plane of her stomach in that window light, her other hand is between her thighs, and it is the one thing in the picture the camera couldn’t keep: it has gone to a blur, moving. She didn’t stop to aim. She didn’t stop.

He lies under the beaded nails with the phone close to his face and his heart going so hard in his ears he thinks it must be audible from Kevin’s mattress. He is hard against the zipper of his jeans, the blood gone heavy and low in him, his free hand shut on a fistful of sleeping bag. He wants her so completely it stops being a thought and becomes weather, the attic gone hot under a cold roof, and half a continent of it between him and that bed.
He answers with one thumb, slowly, the keys going in one letter at a time, because it’s T9, and because the hand isn’t steady.

response.text: opened it alone. in an attic. you win. you always win. now sleep

response: He shuts the phone. From the next mattress, without moving, Theo says, “Go to sleep, Costigan.”

choices.key: At two in the morning in the Broussards’ attic you opened what Skye sent from Vancouver, and then you erased it.
response: He opens it.

It comes down the screen from the top a band at a time, and he tilts it to the streetlight, and he gets the plaid first, his own shirt spread under her for a sheet, and then her face upside down until he turns it: her head back off the pillow, her mouth open, her eyes shut, nobody in it looking at anybody. The frame runs crooked down the bed from above, her own arm across the corner of it. That’s enough. That’s more than enough. His thumb is on the key before the last band has come in.
*Erase this message?*
*Yes.*

It goes off the screen. It doesn’t go anywhere else. He lies there with the heat of it in his face and his body, and his free hand in a fist on the sleeping bag, and waits for his heart to come down out of his ears, and it doesn’t, much. He answers her.

response.text: i looked. then i erased it. house full of people. i wont forget it anyway

response: He shuts the phone. From the next mattress, without moving, Theo says, “Go to sleep, Costigan.”

choices.key: At two in the morning in the Broussards’ attic you deleted what Skye sent from Vancouver without opening it, and told her so, and why.
response: He holds the key down.
*Erase this message?*
*Yes.*

It goes, the envelope and the paperclip and whatever was under them, before he has seen any of it. The texts stay. He lies there and looks at the three of them in the green light with his thumb still on the key, and it costs exactly what he thought it would, and a little more.
He tells her the truth.
